sense: where to sit in a café or restaurant

terms.gloss: Inside or out in the open air?
terms.comment: A question of ours: we have found no set phrase for it in the authors or the reference works searched. It joins intus, inside, with sub dīvō, the classical phrase for “in the open air”. Forīs also means out of doors, but forīs cēnāre is “to eat out”, away from home (see “eat out”), so sub dīvō is clearer here. For a seat by the window, ad fenestram; a roof terrace is sōlārium (see “terrace”).

terms.grammar: sub with the ablative of dīvum, the sky
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.1.51: in silvā dēnique disposita sub dīvō vīdimus
Plin. Ep. 6.16.16: Sub diō rūrsus quamquam levium exēsōrumque pūmicum cāsus metuēbātur
Hor. C. 2.3.23: sub dīvō moreris (Lewis & Short s.v. dīvus)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short s.v. dīvus: “under the open sky, in the open air”. Pliny writes the other form, sub diō.

phrases.english: The sun’s out: let’s eat outside.

phrases.latin: Ad fenestram sedeāmus, ut nāvēs spectēmus.
phrases.english: Let’s sit by the window, so we can watch the boats.

phrases.latin: illa quaerō quae apud tē nūper ad omnīs columnās, omnibus etiam intercolumniīs, in silvā dēnique disposita sub dīvō vīdimus
phrases.english: I am asking about the statues we saw at your house not long ago, at every column, in every space between the columns, even set out in the open air in the grove
